article.title: Scopes Trial
article.author: Berry Craig
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. "The Christian Nationalist Agenda Is Dead," trumpeted the headline in a November 5 Texas Monthly story, though the subhead was a qualifier: "For now, anyway." Christian nationalism is the rock upon which the MAGA church was largely built. "Christian Nationalism may not have been explicitly on the ballot," wrote Robert Downen. "But Anthea Butler, chair of the religious-studies department at the University of Pennsylvania, said it’s hard not to see [Nov. 3] as, at least in part, a rebuke of its hard-line and exclusionary views." To quote the immortal Coach Corso , “Not so fast, my friend.” Related: Jim Crow Said This Could Never Happen: Mayfield Just Elected a Black Mayor One-hundred-one summers ago, modernists, ancestors of today’s progressives, were preaching the funeral of white Protestant fundamentalism, the spiritual fountainhead of Christian nationalism, They were sure the famous Tennessee “Monkey Trial,” had everlastingly discredited what H.L. Mencken, the iconoclastic journalist and social critic, called "degraded nonsense" that "was being rammed and hammered into yokel skulls" by "country preachers." Defendant John Thomas Scopes, a Kentuckian from Paducah, where I was a journalist and community college history professor, was convicted and fined $100 plus court costs because he taught evolution in the public high school in Dayton, Tenn. A Volunteer State law prohibited the teaching of "any theory that denies the story of the Divine Creation of man as taught in the Bible, and to teach instead that man has descended from a lower order of animals.” The law applied to all state-supported schools, including teacher training colleges and the University of Tennessee. The mainstream media narrative held that the guilty verdict aside, “it was fundamentalism that had been intellectually defeated and publicly humiliated,” wrote Michael A. Smith in a Christian Century article marking the centennial of the courtroom battle. Dubbed "The Trial of the Century," it grabbed headlines worldwide. Smith hastened to add, “This narrative of fundamentalist defeat proved premature.” Like the modernists of old, progressives who are thinking, wishfully or otherwise, that the Big Blue Tsunami cleansed the country of Christian nationalism might be jumping the gun. Heretofore, "time and time again, voters responded to the GOP’s open embrace of Christian nationalism, which claims that America was founded as a Christian nation and should have laws that reflect a hard-line conservative version of the faith, by electing members of religious minority groups that would be directly affected by the movement’s sustained success,” wrote Downen, who listed a slew of MAGA Republicans routed in the biggest midterm Democratic blowout in decades. Downen hedged a tad in the last paragraph of his article: “'I think [Christian Nationalists]...are going to have to crawl under a rock and figure out what to do next,' [Prof.] Butler said. But she cautioned against pronouncing Christian nationalism entirely dead—politically speaking, it is a movement that thinks and plots in generations, if not longer.” The irascible Mencken, who covered the trial for The Baltimore Sun, also pilloried William Jennings Bryan, the anti-evolution crusader who was brought in as special prosecutor. HLM lampooned Bryan, a former Democratic congressman, secretary of state and three time presidential candidate, as “the peasants’ Pope.” But he advised, “let no one, laughing at him, underestimate the magic that lies in his black, malignant eye.” Related: Hegseth’s Holy War on Fat Generals Meets the Weight of History The Bad Boy of Baltimore didn’t join the media chorus in claiming that fundamentalism was finished. "Heave an egg out of a Pullman window, and you will hit a Fundamentalist almost everywhere in the United States to-day,” he wrote . “They swarm in the country towns, inflamed by their shamans , and with a saint (Bryan died shortly after the Scopes trial), now, to venerate. They are thick in the mean streets behind the gas-works. They are everywhere where learning is too heavy a burden for mortal minds to carry, even the vague, pathetic learning on tap in little red schoolhouses. They march with the Klan, with the Christian Endeavor Society, with the Junior Order of United American Mechanics, with the Epworth League, with all the rococo bands that poor and unhappy folk organize to bring some light of purpose into their lives. They have had a thrill, and they are ready for more.” Maybe I missed it. But I have yet to hear any MAGA Republican bigwig from Trump down disavow Christian Nationalism or the Christian Nationalist-tinged "Million Crusader Cross March.” Billed as a "peaceful protest & Christian unity against the rigged midterms," the demonstration is set for the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, not coincidentally the day the new Congress is supposed to be sworn in. Marchers are asked to bring crosses, though apparently not flaming ones. “Organizers describe it as a peaceful gathering,” wrote Kevin Slimp for United Methodist Insight online. “But take a look at the promotional material, and you might understand why people are concerned. He posted a copy of a promotional poster that "features medieval armies in armor, paired with language challenging the election results. For those who remember the weeks leading up to January 6, 2021, that combination brings back some troubling memories....None of this tells us what will happen on January 3. But when election grievances, images of armored crusaders, and someone with Lang’s history come together at the Capitol, there’s reason to pay attention.” There is indeed. I've lived in white rural western Kentucky for all my 76 years. Toss an egg from a passing Amtrak in my county or from any moving vehicle just about everywhere in white rural America and you’re likely to bean a Christian Nationalist.
